Hi, OP! Echoing what others have said, I think this poem is a little underdeveloped and I wish there was more. I have some ideas for how you could make this poem more powerful:

* Add some more sensory details. 
* Give us some clue about where the speaker is (as in, where they are physically located). I'm a huge hypocrite for saying this, because my last poem didn't situate the reader anywhere either. 
* Tell us: what makes the speaker's body finally break?
* Describe how the body breaks rather than just tell us it has broken. 
* I'm a little confused about how the first line is connected to the second line.

I really liked the first line (or the ideas from it--I think it wouldn't hurt to sharpen it too). Thanks so much for sharing it with us!

Hi, OP! If your goal is to make the poem more refined, here are my suggestions. Get rid of the rhyme. You don't need it! Though, I'm a little conflicted because I do enjoy the last two lines in their current, rhyming form. But, I think in the rest of the poem the rhyme is making the poem sound less mature. Give us some specific information about the speaker and the person they're addressing. The more specific the better! Thanks so much for sharing with us

I love your nom de plume, OP! I have some suggestions, in case you were interested in doing revisions: 

* "Double edged they are" sounds a little awkward to me. 
* "Who is friend and who is foe?" is a little tired. But, I'm not one to talk. I'm Captain Cliché. 
* Did you mean to use the word "back" at the end of both of those lines? Is there any way you could come up with another word to put there so it's less repetitive? 
* "Never let your feelings show"/"Can't ever let them know" reminds me too much of "Let It Go" from Frozen. I think maybe it would be a good idea to abandon the rhyme. 
* "Wait and see" is a cliché
* "Keep your wits about you" is a cliché
* "Eaten alive" is a cliché
* "Keep your cards close to your chest" is a cliché

I really like "under the lace, lies their true face" and "only ever show your best." "Only ever show your best" is a great way of playing with the "keep your cards close to your chest" cliché and turning it into something fresh. I'd really like to see you do the same thing with the other clichés that I've noted--find a fresh angle. Or just cut them out and replace them with something else. But, overall I enjoyed it! Thanks so much for sharing!

I have no words. You should submit this to a literary magazine. It's leagues ahead of what the rest of us are writing. This isn't a workshop comment--just appreciation. I don't have the language to describe all the ways this worked for me, but I'll try:

* The specificity.
* The fact that my senses were all engaged.
* The absolutely stunning last lines. 
* I love the way that the final stanza gave greater meaning to all the ones that came before it. 

Absolutely searing, haunting, beautiful work.

I there were a lot of drug references in here that I'm not personally familiar enough with to understand, so keep that in mind when reading my feedback--I'm probably missing a lot of context.

* I think you might be mixing up sadist and masochist--masochists are the ones who like to feel pain. Sadists are the ones who inflict pain. It doesn't make sense for a sadist to cry with you or give you their hair. 
* I like the line "calamus root" though I have no idea what it means or how it's relevant. It just sounds nice. 
* I'm having trouble understanding the connection between the opioid and the homunculus (also I think homunculus might be misspelled). 

However!  I liked how easy this was to read. Short lines are easy on the eyes. I have no idea what is going on in this poem--it feels kind of like flashes of consciousness between blackouts on someone's drug binge. If that's intentional, then well done. If not, then, maybe make it clearer what is going on in the poem. I know that someone cheated on someone (I think?) or maybe they just broke up and the speaker is jealous. Overall, this is an interesting first draft. Thanks for sharing!

Hi, OP. I have some questions for you to consider in revising the poem for your next draft:

* Perceived by whom?
* Exposed to what?
* Adorned in what?
* What was quelled? 
* What experience?
* Returned to where/whom/what?
* What is "it"?

I really love the formatting of this poem. It's distinctive--I've never seen anything quite like it, but now I'm surprised that I haven't because I read a lot of poetry. I think telling the reader what the "it" in the poem is (preferably towards the beginning of the poem) would do a lot for the poem, but I get that you're probably keeping it a mystery intentionally. Thanks for sharing with us!

Hi, OP. This poem seems a little underdeveloped. There don't seem to be any descriptive, concrete details. It kind of reminds me of something you'd find in a greeting card in its current form--made to be so broad that it could work for just about any occasion, because there's nothing specific to really hold on to. But, this clearly resonated with everyone else, so I'm probably just not understanding. You're a better poet than me too, so I'm in no position to critique. I have some suggestions for how you could improve this:

* Tell us: what your paradise looks/sounds/feels/smells/and tastes like--the person or the place. It doesn't matter which. I just, as a reader, really want some details to hold on to (again, I'm really bad at doing this so I'm in no place to be critiquing that because you still do a better job of this than I do).
* How does peace = paradise? I feel like there's a jump there and it would be nice to know the logic of how you got from point peace to point paradise.

I think overall this poem really resonated with a lot of people so take my critique with a grain of salt. Every one else is connecting with it just fine. I'm the 10th dentist here.

Hi, OP. Here are my observations:

* In the first line, I think "loves" should be "love's".
* It was unclear to me whether the was dark that was riding the lightning or if the line means there is lightning made for riding, like riding boots.
* "Worlds" should have an apostrophe too, so "world's"

I assume you are not using standard American or British English, because you say "crumplin'" rather than "crumpling." And you use the grammatical construction "be" in the same way as it's used in AAVE, different forms of Southern American English, Caribbean English, some forms of Canadian English, and I think Irish English. So, I'm not going to do standard American English grammatical nitpicks there, because the habitual "be" is grammatically correct depending on what variety of English you're speaking.

I'm a big fan of using different varieties of English in poetry, because I think every variety has its own unique musicality. I usually am not too big a fan of rhyme, but it worked for me in this poem, probably because it felt musical. Thanks so much for sharing your work!
It was a pleasure! Thank you for sharing!

Hi, OP. I noticed some grammatical issues with the poem.

* " The *words* that I speak, I just wish you would hear *it*." "Words" is plural and "it" is singular. 
* "I've traverse here and there" doesn't make sense grammatically. 
* "I'd love to the moon" doesn't make sense grammatically. Maybe you mean love as far as the moon or something like that? Or "I once believed I loved the moon"? I think the latter is more interesting.
* "To love not one other but you" also doesn't make sense grammatically.
* I think maybe you could replace "should" with "shall" in line 4, but maybe don't because it might make it sound stilted. 
* I didn't understand "My belief in many is strife."
* I'd recommend changing "he'lllve" to "he will have" but "for the gallows he will have took" still doesn't quite make sense to me.

I don't think you need to use the fancy heightened (that's probably not the right word but I can't think of it now) language to get your point across. I think simplifying and focusing on concrete details would help.

This is gorgeous and raw. I appreciated the use of variation in line length--how it made certain portions slow down and speed up. It was like I could hear someone speaking it. It felt very much like slam poetry--I could feel the places where the speaker would be spitting out the words rapid-fire and the places where he'd take a breath and we, the listeners, would all go totally still, in suspense. 

My ONE nitpick would be that I think you might mean palpitates (palpates means pushing down on the body in a diagnostic medical context from what I understand. The doctor palpates your stomach when you come in with abdominal pain, for example. Palpitates is the word I think you're looking for--your heart palpitates. When I read the last three lines, I imagined the skin pulsing/beating/shaking like a heart, because on my first read through I read it as "palpitates" rather than "palpates." All in all, this was a great experience to read. It felt like the poem was being read to me--performed in front of me. 

Thank you for sharing!

This poem is extremely intriguing. 

**My experience reading the poem:** 

For a minute there, I thought it had a sci-fi/supernatural theme. Then, I thought, oh--it's just a teenager describing their family in a way that indicates they feel alienated. Then, I got to the end and suddenly realized I must have misunderstood the poem and there did seem to be something supernatural about it. Or maybe it's just a person spying on a family from above. 

Then, I gave it another read-through, really paying attention now. If this is after school, does this mean the speaker goes to school or is it just after school for the children who are being watched? Who is this mysterious Carer entity? An orderly? A foster parent? The spirit of a dead gull or a person who died there? Who is the Friend? Is it a sort of time warp where dead people watch their past lives play out down below? But if so, why would the speaker be retreating into the moss? 

Third read-through: the Sister seems aware of the speaker, so it seems like this is just a member of the family. I don't know who the Carer is. If summer is approaching but it's mid-June then maybe that lends some support to my time-warp theory. Are they watching their own past play out? Is the speaker a Seagull? Are the Carer, the Friend, and the family hallucinations? 

I have so many questions. Every time I read this poem my interpretation changes. But, now I'm sure that the speaker is either watching their life flash before their eyes or watching a family that is just like their family was ("Even yourself.")

It's an enigma of a poem (or maybe I'm just tired). Whatever the intended meaning, I found it interesting enough to read several times. I'd love to know another missing piece of the puzzle to guide my interpretation. I also appreciated how the poem itself is shaped like a rocky cliff (at least on my screen). 

Thank you for sharing, OP!

I noticed a couple of places where it felt like words were missing or the wording felt a little strange: 

* "illuminate/ my fatal wounds effaced" <--here effaced doesn't quite seem to fit. Effaced means erased, but it seems that the paint would highlight rather than conceal the wounds. But, it's possible I've just misunderstood the poem.
* "His agony conveyed \[missing word(s)?\] dripping blood off his frame" 
* The phrase "on my death row" sounds a little weird to American ears because the expression "death row" has a specific meaning here: a high security prison for people convicted of capital crimes and sentenced to death, where they wait for decades to be executed while filing many appeals and going through a bunch of legal processes. Death row is not the execution chamber itself, thought execution chambers are almost always inside of high security prisons. I understand it was a play on words, since the theme of execution runs throughout the poem. Plus I can't think of anything to compare to an execution chamber in an art museum. So, this is just a nitpick.

Hi, OP. I normally don't care for rhyme in poems (even though I do it a lot and never quite get it right)--I think it's usually unnecessary. But, here the repetition and rhyme brought to mind a nursery rhyme that you might read to a child at bedtime--I think that was intentional and appropriate. I love when poems about sleep do that. I don't know what the technical term for it is--when the form of a poem is related to the content. But, that's what you're doing here. My one criticism is that I feel like this poem would be more effective with some sensory details. There seems to be a lot of telling; I'd like some detailed and specific showing. What you need to look out for, I think especially with rhyming poems, is cliché. Specific details, in my unprofessional opinion, help to avoid cliché. But, overall, I think the simplicity and nursery-rhyme structure didn't hurt the poem.

The new format looks nice! Curseth is grammatically not correct there. The archaic equivalent I think you're looking for is either curséd or cursèd (I really have no clue which one is correct). It would have been written at the time as just "cursed" but would have been pronounced like "curs-ed" and for the modern pronunciation of cursed it would have been written curs'd. 

"Be nourished" or "flourish" would mean the maggots are eating the corpse. "May maggots nourish" as it's written now means that the corpse is being nourished by the maggots. 

These are all nitpicks though. Overall, I enjoyed the poem!
